entry.title: Ankle Foot Orthosis Intervention Improves the Ground Reaction Forces During Walking in Patients with Peripheral Artery Disease (Randomized Clinical Trial).
entry.content:
Salamifar Z, Fallahtafti F, Samson K, Pipinos II, et al. · Actuators · 2026

This study investigated the impact of walking with ankle-foot-orthoses (AFOs) and without AFOs (non-AFO) on ground reaction forces (GRFs) in patients with peripheral artery disease (PAD). Additionally, this study examined the effect of AFO intervention vs. no AFO intervention on GRFs while walking with and without AFOs. Fifty patients with PAD were randomly assigned to either a three-month intervention (AFO) or a control (standard-of-care) group. After three months, subjects crossed over to the alternate group and were evaluated after three additional months. GRF data (anterior-posterior, medial-lateral, and vertical) were collected during walking with and without AFOs at baseline, three, and six months. Peak discrete GRF points, braking and propulsion impulses were compared across conditions, groups, and time points using linear mixed models. The peak brake and propulsion GRF were significantly reduced while walking with AFOs versus non-AFO (p < 0.01). Compared to non-AFO, walking with AFOs significantly reduced lateral GRF magnitude (p = 0.03) and significantly increased medial GRF (p = 0.02). The first and second maximum (p < 0.01) vertical GRF were significantly increased with AFOs versus non-AFOs. Walking with AFOs helped patients with PAD achieve greater peak propulsion and vertical GRFs compared to non-AFO, with GRF values trending toward those previously reported in healthy individuals.

entry.title: How Effectively Does Protective Sports Gear Prevent Sports Injuries?
entry.content:
Jami M, Mujadzic T, Marcelli AL, Netscher DTJ · South Med J · 2026

As organized and recreational sports continue to grow in popularity, associated sports injuries increasingly burden athletes. Protective sports gear is intended to reduce injury risk during play. This article provides a comprehensive review of the mechanism and efficacy of protective sports gear in injury prevention to the head and neck, upper extremity, and lower extremity and assesses where perhaps evidence for protection is lacking. Helmets, face shields, and protective eyewear have clear benefits in structural protection against injury. The impact of sports gear in reducing sport-related concussion is more variable, largely due to the repetitive nature of the injury mechanism where cumulative low-magnitude impacts contribute to brain injury. For the upper extremity, wrist guards have a clear benefit in reducing major and minor injuries among gymnasts and snowboarders and hence by inference on other impact sports. Ankle braces and taping potentially reduce the risk of ankle sprains among athletes, and the mandating of shin guards in professional soccer results in decreased sports-related lower extremity fractures. Further research is warranted to evaluate the effectiveness of sports gear on reinjury prevention and to study the implications of sports gear on risk compensation theory in athletes.

entry.title: Feedforward neuromuscular control and dynamic postural stability in people with chronic ankle instability during single-leg landing.
entry.content:
Li TY, Wang Z, Cascoe R, Aki-Sawyerr J, et al. · J Biomech · 2026

Individuals with chronic ankle instability(CAI) show deficits in neuromuscular control and postural stability. While feedback mechanisms are well-studied, feedforward mechanisms during dynamic tasks remains underexplored. This study compared feedforward neuromuscular control and dynamic postural stability among CAI, coper and healthy groups. Fifteen CAI(23.5 ± 2.9 years, 11 M/4F), fifteen coper(24.1 ± 3.4 years, 12 M/3F) and fifteen healthy participants(25.5 ± 3.5 years, 11 M/4F) performed single-leg drop landings from 30 cm. Total centre of pressure movement during 1-second and 3-second(TOTEX1s&TOTEX3s), mediolateral sway distance(DML), peak vertical GRF(peak vGRF) and root-mean-square of mediolateral GRF in the first 0.4 s(RMS_ML_0.4) were recorded via force plate. Surface electromyography recorded muscle activity 200 ms before landing among tibialis anterior(TA), peroneus longus(PL) and gastrocnemius lateralis(GL). Pre-activation timing was calculated using the Teager-Kaiser energy operator(TKEO). Statistical analysis involved one-way ANOVA(α = 0.05) and Tukey post-hoc testing. Compared to healthy participants, CAI individuals displayed earlier TA(270 ± 73 ms vs. 85 ± 53 ms, p < 0.001) and PL(260 ± 87 ms vs. 102 ± 62 ms, p < 0.001) pre-activations, alongside higher TA activity(76 ± 27% vs. 35 ± 19%, p < 0.001) but lower PL activity(38 ± 14% vs. 77 ± 23%, p < 0.001). Higher RMS_ML_0.4(6.7 ± 1.3%BW vs. 5.6 ± 1.0%BW, p = 0.037), DML(55.6 ± 15.7 mm vs. 39.5 ± 9.0 mm, p < 0.001) and peak vGRF(334 ± 44%BW vs. 286 ± 59%BW, p = 0.041)were observed as well. Coper showed earlier GL pre-activation(169 ± 57 ms vs. 108 ± 67 ms, p = 0.021), increased activity(155 ± 40% vs. 97 ± 29%, p < 0.001) and decreased DML(42.7 ± 7.0 mm vs. 55.6 ± 15.7 mm, p = 0.008) compared to CAI individuals. CAI exhibited postural control deficits and ineffective feedforward control, shown by lower PL activity despite early pre-activation. Rate of force production training is advised. Increased GL activation may serve as a compensatory response in copers after initial ankle sprain.

entry.title: [Sensorimotor insoles for musculoskeletal disorders : An evidence-based rapid review].
entry.content:
Walther M, Greitemann B, Kerkoff A, Seeßle M, et al. · Orthopadie (Heidelb) · 2026

Sensorimotor foot orthoses (SMFOs) are designed to modulate afferent input through targeted plantar stimuli and thereby influence neuromuscular control mechanisms. This review aimed to provide an evidence-based assessment of their clinical effectiveness across different musculoskeletal conditions. We conducted a rapid review of randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews. We evaluated the available evidence for different orthotic concepts on an indication-specific basis using the GRADE approach. The strongest evidence was for symptomatic flexible pes planovalgus and patellofemoral pain syndrome, although no consistent superiority of SMFOs over conventional supportive foot orthoses was demonstrated. In patients with patellofemoral pain syndrome, randomized data showed significant improvements in pain and function with both SMFOs and conventional foot orthoses. For chronic ankle instability, the evidence regarding sensorimotor interventions is largely limited to mechanistic and indirect outcomes. Interpretation is further complicated because the textured insoles used in many studies do not match what is traditionally understood as SMFOs in German-speaking orthopedic practice. Evidence for SMFOs in nonspecific low back pain is even more limited and is characterized by heterogeneous findings. Based on the current literature, no clear superiority of sensorimotor orthotic concepts can be demonstrated for any specific diagnosis. However, this should not be interpreted as evidence of general ineffectiveness. SMFOs represent a therapeutic option within multimodal treatment strategies and should be prescribed according to the individual indication and patient-specific treatment goals.

entry.title: Effects of sensorimotor training combined with short foot exercise on knee and ankle gait kinematics in individuals with flatfoot: A preliminary study.
entry.content:
Moon DC, Jung JH · Medicine (Baltimore) · 2026

Flatfoot, a common condition characterized by medial longitudinal arch collapse, alters foot and lower-limb mechanics. Sensorimotor training and short-foot exercises can improve postural stability and functional performance. However, their combined effects on gait kinematics remain unclear. This preliminary study evaluated the 6-week effects of combining these interventions on knee and ankle gait kinematics in individuals with flexible flatfeet. Thirty-two asymptomatic young adults with flexible flatfoot (14 males, 18 females; navicular drop ≥ 10 mm) were randomly assigned to an experimental group (sensorimotor training combined with short-foot exercises; n = 16) or a control group (sensorimotor training only; n = 16) using sealed opaque envelopes. Training was conducted 3 times per week for 6 weeks in a motion laboratory. Gait kinematics were assessed pre- and post-intervention using the VICON motion system. Outcomes included peak ankle inversion, eversion, dorsiflexion, and plantarflexion angles, knee internal and external rotation angles, and range of motion (ROM) in the sagittal, frontal, and transverse planes. Two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance was used for the analysis. The partial eta squared (ηp2) was reported as the effect size. Baseline demographics (age, sex, and body mass index) were similar between groups (P > .05). Significant group × time interactions were observed for gait variables. The experimental group showed a significant increase in peak ankle inversion (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.53-2.71; P = .004; ηp2 = 0.244) and a decrease in peak eversion (95% CI: 1.68-4.89; P = .002; ηp2 = 0.279). Peak knee internal rotation significantly decreased (95% CI: -9.92 to -2.82; P = .006; ηp2 = 0.228). Reductions were also observed in sagittal plane ankle ROM (95% CI: -4.88 to -0.68; P = .001; ηp2 = 0.317) and transverse plane knee ROM (95% CI: -7.75 to -4.01; P = .003; ηp2 = 0.254). No significant changes were found in ankle dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, knee external rotation, or frontal plane ankle ROM (P = .088, .126, .766, .136, respectively; ηp2 = 0.003-0.094). Combined sensorimotor and short-foot training more effectively improved gait kinematics than sensorimotor training alone, suggesting a promising non-surgical approach for managing flatfoot.

entry.title: Ankle Proprioceptive Performance on Increasingly Challenging Functional Tasks in Groups With and Without Chronic Ankle Instability.
entry.content:
Wang X, Shao X, Shi X, Adams RD, et al. · J Sport Rehabil · 2026

Up to 75% of lateral ankle sprain cases experience long-term impairments and suffer chronic ankle instability (CAI), a condition characterized by impaired ankle proprioception. This study aims to investigate ankle proprioceptive performance during functional tasks with increasing movement control and ankle joint load in individuals with and without CAI. Cross-sectional study. Twenty individuals with CAI and 19 healthy controls completed 4 proprioceptive tasks: standing, walking, landing (double-leg drop), and stair descent. In each task, their ability to discriminate between 4 ankle inversion angles was assessed using a task-specific discrimination apparatus. CAI participants had significantly lower ankle proprioception scores than controls (mean difference = 0.047, 95% CI, 0.031-0.063). Proprioceptive acuity varied by task (P < .001, ηp2=.345), with no significant group-by-task interaction (P = .220, ηp2=.039). Trend analysis showed a linear improvement in proprioceptive performance with increasing ankle load and challenge in controls (P < .001, ηp2=.685), whereas the CAI group showed both significant linear (P < .001, ηp2=.445) and quadratic (P = .001, ηp2=.430) trends, reflecting a rise followed by a significant downturn as load peaked. Both groups improved with greater load, but during stair descent, individuals with CAI exhibited a significant decline. This suggests that proprioceptive processing in CAI is impaired and may be overloaded during highly challenging tasks.

entry.title: Gait speed and multi-segment foot joint kinematics throughout the entire stance phase using statistical parametric mapping.
entry.content:
Jeong H, Hamill J, Boyer KA, van Emmerik REA · PeerJ · 2026

The foot is a multi-segment structure whose segments function together. Due to its ongoing connection with the support surface, the foot must be capable of managing loads that vary with gait speed. Previous studies have provided considerable insight into the relationship between foot joint kinematics and gait speed. However, their primary reliance on discrete measures, such as peak joint angles, has limited understanding of how these relationships evolve throughout the stance phase. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of gait speed on full time-series trajectories of multiplanar foot joint kinematics using statistical parametric mapping. According to our findings, faster walking primarily increased ankle eversion and midfoot dorsiflexion during weight acceptance (∼17-29% of the stance phase). In contrast, during propulsion, faster walking increased ankle plantar flexion (∼80-100% of the stance phase) and inversion (∼82-90%), as well as midfoot plantar flexion (∼82-100%) and adduction (∼90-98%), together with greater dorsiflexion of the first metatarsophalangeal joint after heel-off (∼43-98% of the stance phase). These multiplanar joint kinematic alterations across the ankle-foot joints throughout the stance phase reflect greater foot-arch collapse in early stance and foot-arch recoil in late stance, which may facilitate appropriate energy absorption and generation in response to increasing gait speed. Importantly, these adaptive foot motions were not captured by previous discrete analyses, which may obscure phase-dependent changes during gait. The present continuous time-series approach revealed detailed temporal adaptations in foot kinematics across the stance phase, providing a more comprehensive characterization of gait mechanics.

entry.title: Using Wearable Sensors and Video Analysis to Improve Functional Electrical Stimulation Prescription in Individuals With Multiple Sclerosis: A Case Series.
entry.content:
Jackson K, Hosseini S, Bigelow K · Int J MS Care · 2026

A growing body of evidence supports the use of functional electrical stimulation (FES) in people with multiple sclerosis (MS). However, prescription remains an imprecise process with no well-established guidelines for assessing the immediate or long-term effects to ensure maximum benefit. The purpose of this case series was to assess the potential benefits of using wearable sensors and video analysis to provide immediate feedback on gait performance to improve FES prescription in people with MS. Three adults (2 women, 1 man; age range, 39-62 years) with MS with varying levels of lower extremity motor function and gait impairment were enrolled. During a single visit, participants performed a series of 10-m walks under various FES and non-FES conditions while using wearable motion sensors. Additionally, 2D video analysis was used to assess alterations in knee angles during swing and stance phases. All participants demonstrated improvements in a variety of gait variables, including a clinically meaningful (> 0.1 m/s) increase in gait speed during 1 or more of the FES conditions when compared with the no-device and/or prescribed ankle foot orthosis conditions. There were additional improvements associated with multichannel stimulation of the lower leg and thigh for certain gait variables. Data from the wearable sensors and video analysis were advantageous in helping researchers determine the most appropriate FES prescription for each participant. This case series demonstrates the potential clinical usefulness of these technologies in prescribing FES for people with MS.

entry.title: [Posttraumatic ankle arthrofibrosis : Diagnosis, prevention and treatment].
entry.content:
Al-Qaysi B, Winter P, Landgraeber S, Wagener J, et al. · Unfallchirurgie (Heidelb) · 2026

Posttraumatic arthrofibrosis is a rare cause of painful motion loss after injury or surgery, with limited available evidence. Posttraumatic arthrofibrosis is characterized by painful, progressive stiffness with more than 30% loss of motion and no major radiographic abnormality. Reported rates range from 2% to 10% after ankle injuries to up to 73% after surgically treated fractures, while ankle-specific data on risk factors remain limited. The pathogenesis appears to involve transforming growth factor (TGF)-β, interleukin (IL)-1, and hypoxia-mediated capsular fibrosis. Arthrography remains the diagnostic gold standard according to the Goldman criteria. Magnetic resonance imaging may show capsular thickening ≥ 3 mm and stage-dependent signal changes. First-line treatment comprises physiotherapy, mobilization, and dynamic or static progressive orthoses. A mean 17° gain in total range of motion was reported with static progressive orthoses. In refractory stiffness, arthroscopic capsular release may be beneficial, with improvement of the American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS) score from 63.8 to 88.6, dorsiflexion from 1 to 19°, and acceptable motion in more than 80% of patients. Posttraumatic arthrofibrosis of the ankle is rare, underdiagnosed, and treatable. Early recognition and stepwise conservative treatment, followed by arthroscopic capsular release, may restore function. The evidence is based mainly on small level IV studies. Prospective studies are required.

entry.title: Auditory Biofeedback Gait Training in Individuals With Chronic Ankle Instability: Protocol for a Randomized Controlled Trial.
entry.content:
Torp DM, Choi JY, Edison A, Hoch M, et al. · JMIR Res Protoc · 2026

Chronic ankle instability (CAI) develops in a large majority of patients with lateral ankle sprain (LAS), who often experience recurring injuries, residual feelings of instability, and abnormal neuromuscular patterns. Specifically, gait alterations are common in those with CAI and considered a contributing factor to poor long-term ankle joint health. Yet, there are no evidence-based gait-training protocols targeted to improve biomechanics, which may improve long-term outcomes related to ankle joint health and patient satisfaction. This study protocol introduces a progressive auditory biofeedback (ABF) gait-training program aimed to improve short- and long-term lower extremity biomechanics and talar cartilage outcomes and reduce the frequency of ankle-giving-way episodes and recurring injuries. This study is a multisite randomized controlled trial (RCT) with a target enrollment of 100 patients with CAI into a control group (n=50, 50%) or an ABF gait-training program (n=50, 50%). Both groups will complete a progressive 6-week (12-session) protocol comprising walking, ruck marching, and running on a treadmill. Lower extremity kinematics and kinetics, talar cartilage characteristics (via ultrasonography), self-perceived dysfunction and instability, and number of recurring sprains will be assessed prior to intervention, immediately after intervention, and 6 and 12 months postintervention. Finally, the frequency of ankle-giving-way episodes in the 6 months prior to intervention will be compared to the frequency of episodes at the 6- and 12-month time points to determine a longitudinal difference in ankle-giving-way episodes. The study was funded in September 2024 and prospectively registered through ClinicalTrials.gov on March 10, 2025. The first participant was enrolled in May 2025. As of August 2026, 118 individuals had been recruited and 19 participants enrolled. Recruitment will remain open until September 2027, and study completion is expected in September 2028. Data processing is projected to continue through September 2028, with the final report published in June 2029. This study will be the first RCT of ABF gait training to assess the immediate and long-term effects on lower extremity biomechanics, ankle joint health, and patient-reported outcomes in patients with CAI. Results from this study will advance the knowledge of long-term joint health that may be associated with poor outcomes post-LAS. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06868316; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06868316. DERR1-10.2196/107775.

entry.title: Pain-stratified differences in lower-limb mechanics and neuromuscular activation during single-leg drop landing in male athletes with chronic ankle instability.
entry.content:
Wang Z, Zheng W, Zhou Z, Wang X · Phys Ther Sport · 2026

To compare mechanical and neuromuscular strategies between high- and low-pain subgroups of male athletes with chronic ankle instability (CAI) during single-leg drop landing. Cross-sectional study. Biomechanics laboratory. Eighty-four male Tier 2-3 athletes, stratified into high-pain CAI (n = 28), low-pain CAI (n = 28), and healthy control (n = 28) groups. Lower-limb kinematics, impact loading, joint moments, eccentric work and energy contributions, surface electromyographic root mean square amplitude, and co-contraction index. Significant group effects were observed for kinematic outcomes (p ≤ 0.042; ηp2 = 0.075-0.384), joint kinetics and energetics (p ≤ 0.042; ηp2 = 0.075-0.561), and neuromuscular outcomes (p = 0.005-0.017; ηp2 = 0.096-0.124). The high-pain CAI group exhibited lower ankle plantarflexor moment than both comparison groups (both p < 0.001; d = 1.192-1.210), lower ankle eccentric work (p ≤ 0.001; d = 1.030-1.853), lower ankle energy contribution (p ≤ 0.002; d = 0.983-2.133), and greater knee energy contribution (both p < 0.001; d = 1.209-1.818). The low-pain CAI group exhibited less hip flexion and greater ankle plantarflexion at initial contact and greater ankle dorsiflexion range of motion (p ≤ 0.024; d = 0.736-1.398). The high-pain CAI group showed greater tibialis anterior activation than the low-pain group (p = 0.004; d = 0.903) and greater rectus femoris-biceps femoris co-contraction than controls (p = 0.045; d = 0.672). External impact-loading measures did not differ among groups (p = 0.114-0.265; ηp2 = 0.032-0.058). Pain-defined CAI subgroups differed in interjoint load sharing and selected neuromuscular measures despite comparable external impact loading.

entry.title: Association of Ankle Joint Moment and Ankle Joint Velocity With 60° Ipsilateral Change-of-Direction Performance.
entry.content:
Chen CH, Yeh M, Liu C, Tseng YJ, et al. · J Strength Cond Res · 2026

Chen, C-H, Yeh, M-C, Liu, C, Tseng, Y-J, and Lu, S-T. Association of ankle joint moment and ankle joint velocity with 60° ipsilateral change-of-direction performance. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The rapid acceleration and deceleration associated with a change of direction (COD) is associated with high ankle loading, including high ankle moment and velocity, which have been linked to ankle sprain or chronic ankle instability. Although the correlations between ankle joint loading and contralateral COD (contra-COD) have been investigated, one study reported that ipsilateral COD (ipsi-COD) and contra-COD involve distinct, asymmetrical mechanisms. Therefore, the aim of this study is to evaluate the associations of ankle joint moment and ankle joint velocity with 60° ipsi-COD performance. Thirty-five male athletes of recreational team sports performed an ipsi-COD task with their nondominant leg. A three-dimensional motion-capture system and a force platform were used to collect biomechanical data. Ground contact time was negatively associated with plantarflexion moment (r = -0.511) and inversion moment (r = -0.424). By contrast, horizontal impulse was positively correlated with plantarflexion moment (r = 0.407). No correlation was observed between ground contact time and ground reaction force. The moderate negative correlations of ground contact time with plantarflexion moment and inversion moment suggest that increasing ipsi-COD performance may result in high ankle moments and potentially excessive ankle loading. In addition, the absence of a correlation between ground contact time and GRF suggests that athletes consider focusing on converting their approaching velocity to the intended direction during ipsi-COD, as this study indicates that ground reaction force and impulse are not associated with ipsi-COD performance.

entry.title: Side-Step Cutting Foot Biomechanics and Intrinsic Foot Muscle Sizes in People With Chronic Ankle Instability.
entry.content:
Peters-Dickie JL, Detrembleur C, Lobet S, Deschamps K · J Foot Ankle Res · 2026

Lateral ankle sprains commonly occur during directional changes and often lead to chronic ankle instability (CAI) associated with altered movement patterns, muscle weakness and atrophy. This study aimed to compare foot joint biomechanics during cutting among individuals with CAI, copers, and uninjured controls and to explore the relationship between intrinsic foot muscle sizes and functional status. Cross-sectional study. Sixty-nine recreationally active males (25.4 ± 4 years) were categorised by perceived instability and self-reported function. Ankle and foot joint kinematics and kinetics were assessed using a multi-segment foot model during 45° side-step cutting at a mean approach speed of 3.5 m·s-1. Groups were compared using ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis tests, and continuous biomechanical data were analysed using statistical parametric or non-parametric mapping. Cross-sectional area and thickness of the abductor hallucis and flexor digitorum brevis were recorded using ultrasound imaging. Muscle sizes were explored using general linear models, and correlations with questionnaire scores and physical examination outcomes were calculated. Foot joint kinematics and kinetics did not significantly differ between the groups. Individuals with CAI exhibited lower peak posterior ground reaction force than controls (mean difference: -6.2% of body weight, 95% CI: -11.9 to -0.4, p = 0.03). Statistical parametric mapping revealed lower posterior ground reaction forces from 22% to 46% of stance in CAI versus controls (p < 0.05). Intrinsic foot muscle sizes showed weak, statistically significant negative correlations with perceived instability scores (ρ = -0.31 to -0.36) and self-reported function scores (ρ = -0.26 to -0.33). Despite pronounced sensory-perceptual impairments, individuals with CAI demonstrated few differences in foot joint biomechanics compared with copers and controls during a moderate-speed anticipated cutting task. Reduced braking forces may reflect altered deceleration strategies. These findings suggest the importance of assessing deceleration abilities in people with CAI and indicate a potential role of foot muscles in CAI-related functional outcomes. ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05815576).

entry.title: Feedforward Pre-Activation of Lateral Ankle Muscles Is Insufficient Against Excessive Ankle Inversion During Perturbation in Individuals With Chronic Ankle Instability.
entry.content:
Ran W, Song Q, Yin W · J Foot Ankle Res · 2026

This study aimed to compare ankle kinematics and muscle activation between individuals with and without chronic ankle instability (CAI), both prior to and following landing on an inversion trapdoor during walking, with a particular focus on the feedforward pre-activation of lateral ankle muscles and the consequent ankle kinematics post-perturbation. Forty participants were enrolled, including 20 with CAI and 20 age- and sex-matched non-CAI controls. They walked at their own pace on a custom-designed walking platform equipped with a trapdoor programmed to trigger a 24° inversion perturbation, simulating lateral ankle sprain conditions, across three unanticipated trials. Their lower limb muscle electromyography and ankle kinematics were synchronously collected 200 ms pre- and 200 ms post-perturbation. Continuous between-group data were compared by independent sample t-tests. CAI individuals showed higher pre-activation in the peroneus longus (-200.0 to -196.4 ms, mean diff: -11.38%, p = 0.049; -54.6 to -11.0 ms, mean diff: -10.60%, p = 0.011) and the lateral gastrocnemius (-200.0 to -175.4 ms, mean diff: -7.62%, p = 0.029) prior to perturbation, and lower activation in the peroneus longus at 72.1 to 98.0 ms (mean diff: 17.46%, p = 0.029) post-perturbation. They also showed greater ankle inversion in four clusters post-perturbation (0 to 111.0 ms, mean diff: -4.85°, p < 0.001; 117.0 to 128.0 ms, mean diff: -1.83°, p = 0.020; 142.0 to 145.0 ms, mean diff: -1.30°, p = 0.047; 154.0 to 165.0 ms, mean diff: -1.05°, p = 0.019). CAI individuals exhibit higher feedforward pre-activation in lateral ankle muscles, which may be insufficient against excessive ankle inversion after landing on a trapdoor during walking.

entry.title: Comparison of unisegment and multisegment foot models in ankle biomechanics and distal foot power calculations in individuals with a partial foot amputation.
entry.content:
Dami A, Acien M, Isabelle PL, Moisan G · J Biomech · 2026

Multisegment foot models (MFMs) provide a more detailed assessment of foot biomechanics than conventional unisegment foot models (UFMs), yet their added value in individuals with a partial foot amputation remains unclear. The aim of this study was to compare the modified Oxford MFM to a conventional UFM during the stance phase of walking in individuals with a partial foot amputation. Fourteen adults with toe(s) or ray(s) amputation underwent an instrumented gait analysis using force plates and a three-dimensional motion capture system. Joint angles, moments and power were calculated using inverse dynamics and compared for each individual percentage of the stance phase using one-dimensional statistical parametric mapping. Greater ankle plantarflexion angles across the entire stance phase and greater ankle abduction angles during midstance were observed with the UFM compared with the MFM. Conversely, smaller ankle plantarflexion, inversion, and abduction moments, as well as smaller total support moments across most of the stance phase were observed with the UFM compared with the MFM. Smaller ankle and distal foot power absorption and generation during most of the stance phase, and greater distal foot power generation during pre-swing were observed with the UFM. These findings suggest that modeling the foot as a single rigid segment may alter the interpretation of foot and ankle biomechanics in individuals with a partial foot amputation by alternatively estimating intra-foot structures contribution to propulsion. The MFM may provide a distinct representation of energy restitution, supporting its use for clinical measurement and the assessment of interventions specifically targeting forefoot mechanics.

entry.title: Impact of foot orthoses hindfoot and forefoot wedges on foot and ankle kinematics: A cadaveric study.
entry.content:
Chaverot R, Effatparvar MR, Acien M, Sobczak S, et al. · Foot (Edinb) · 2026

Foot orthoses (FOs) are widely prescribed to manage musculoskeletal and inflammatory disorders affecting the lower limbs by modifying foot and ankle biomechanics. While the addition of medial wedges to FOs is believed to enhance control of pronation-related movements, few studies have quantified their isolated kinematic effects under controlled experimental conditions. The use of cadaveric models allows for precise measurement of bone motion without soft tissue artifacts. Therefore, this study aimed to quantify the effects of 3D-printed FOs with and without a medial hindfoot-forefoot wedge on foot and ankle kinematics in cadaveric specimens during quasi-dynamic loading. It was hypothesized that a medial hindfoot-forefoot wedge would better prevent both forefoot dorsiflexion and ankle eversion in cadaveric specimens. Nine fresh-frozen lower limbs were tested under three randomized conditions: shoe-only (control), standard FOs (SFO), and medial hindfoot-forefoot wedge FOs (MWFO). FOs were 3D printed in PA11 using the multi-jet fusion technology. Specimens were mounted on a mechanical press with simulated muscle tension applied through tendon loading. Kinematic data were collected via a six-camera motion capture system and reflective markers attached to bone-anchored rods. Ankle and forefoot/hindfoot angles and ranges of motion were calculated in the sagittal, frontal, and transverse planes. Non-parametric Friedman ANOVAs and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used to assess between-condition differences (α < 0.05). Compared to the control condition, MWFOs significantly reduced peak ankle dorsiflexion (1.40° ± 3.76° vs 3.54° ± 2.74°, p < 0.001) and increased ankle inversion (9.12° ± 11.13° vs 7.09° ± 11.73°, p = 0.002). MWFOs also increased forefoot/hindfoot plantarflexion (p = 0.018) and adduction (p = 0.018) relative to the control condition. No significant differences in joint range of motion were observed across conditions. The addition of a hindfoot-forefoot medial wedge to 3D-printed FOs modifies ankle and midfoot kinematics under quasi-dynamic loading, primarily by reducing pronation-related movements such as dorsiflexion and eversion. These findings support the biomechanical rationale for incorporating hindfoot-forefoot medial wedges in FOs design to enhance control of foot and ankle motion.

entry.title: Effects of Cognitive Loading on Biomechanical and Cognitive-Motor Performance During Jump Landing-Cutting in Chronic Ankle Instability.
entry.content:
Wang S, Song K, Song I, Kim N, et al. · J Athl Train · 2026

Individuals with chronic ankle instability (CAI) demonstrate a high recurrence rate of ankle sprains during sports activities, even after clinical rehabilitation, suggesting altered biomechanical and cognitive-motor performance under demanding conditions. These deficits may be further exacerbated during dynamic movements under cognitive load. However, previous dual-task studies in individuals with CAI have largely examined biomechanical or cognitive-motor performance outcomes separately, leaving their integrated effects insufficiently understood. To identify delayed reaction time and increased task failures under visuospatial cognitive load in individuals with CAI compared with healthy controls and to investigate associated changes in lower-extremity kinematics and ground reaction forces during a jump landing-cutting task. Cross-sectional study. University research laboratory. Thirty-two physically active participants were included: 16 individuals with CAI (age = 24.81 ± 2.69 years) and 16 healthy controls (age = 24.00 ± 1.75 years). Participants performed jump landing-cutting tasks under a single-task condition and a visuospatial cognitive-task condition using a FitLight (FitLight Corp) system. Lower-extremity kinematics, ground reaction forces, and failure counts were assessed in both conditions; reaction time was assessed only in the cognitive-task condition. The CAI group demonstrated delayed reaction time compared with healthy controls during the cognitive-task condition (P = .033); however, reaction time in the CAI group decreased across repeated trials (P = .013). Both groups committed more failures in the cognitive-task condition than in the single-task condition (P < .001, ηp2 = 0.45). No significant interactions were observed in terms of biomechanical variables (P > .05). Individuals with CAI exhibited clear cognitive-motor deficits under cognitive load, whereas their characteristic biomechanical movement patterns remained unchanged. These findings suggest that cognitive-motor dysfunction may not be adequately captured by biomechanical assessments alone and that integrating both domains may improve evaluation and return-to-play decision-making.

entry.title: The effect of sex-specific footwear on cutting patterns in adolescent female soccer players.
entry.content:
Chen K, Wilkie E, Herrera N, Morelli M, et al. · Sports Biomech · 2026

Sex differences have been identified in foot morphology and soccer-specific movement patterns. However, female-specific athletic footwear has only emerged recently, and research has yet to fully understand its impact on cutting patterns. This study examined the impact of female-specific soccer shoes and unisex soccer shoes on joint kinematics during cutting in adolescent soccer players. Thirty-two females completed unanticipated sidesteps at 45 ± 10 degrees, in both shoe conditions, captured using a markerless motion captures system. Principal component (PC) analysis and hierarchical linear model examined joint angle features against shoe conditions. PCs (PC1, PC2, PC3) represented either differences in joint angle amplitude or a change in angles between different cutting phases. Ankle findings related to greater dorsiflexion and inversion angles throughout cutting (PC1) and during midstance (PC2, PC3) in the female shoe than the unisex shoe. Knee findings related to lower flexion angles during the pre-contact/early cutting phase in the female shoe (PC2). Overall, the female shoe trended towards more optimal inversion, but riskier dorsiflexion and knee flexion patterns for knee injuries. However, direct indications to injury and performance require further exploration. Nonetheless, the presence of kinematic influences in sex-specific soccer footwear designs provides valuable insights for future research directions and footwear development.

entry.title: Breaking out of the mould-recent developments in 3D-printed ankle-foot orthoses and strategies to improve clinical practicality: a systematic review.
entry.content:
Chen JYS, Yam MGJ · Singapore Med J · 2026

Conventional ankle-foot orthoses (C-AFOs) are commonly used to improve patient mobility. The traditional handmade process offers limited design flexibility and personalisation. In the last decade, 3D-printed AFOs (3D-AFOs) have emerged as a promising alternative. While numerous biomechanical benefits over C-AFOs have been suggested, their clinical application and real-world feasibility remain underexplored. This study aims to evaluate recent developments in 3D-AFOs and identify strategies to improve their clinical relevance and integration. A systematic review was conducted on 3 October 2024. Five electronic databases (PubMed, Cochrane, Scopus, CINAHL and EMBASE) were searched for studies published between 2022 and 2024. The inclusion criteria focused on physically tested 3D-AFOs modelled from leg scans or commercial templates. Data were categorised into design, mechanical properties, walking ability and participant satisfaction. Of the 69 studies identified, 11 met the eligibility criteria and 36 participants were included. 3D-AFOs were designed with reduced weight and demonstrated improved gait symmetry and ankle range of motion. The modifiable material composition of 3D-AFOs influenced stiffness and durability. 3D-AFOs also demonstrated improved walking speed and muscle efficiency, although performance varied across terrains. Although superior in comfort, support and effectiveness, 3D-AFOs were comparable or inferior in social participation, perceived weight and convenience of use. While 3D-AFOs demonstrate strong biomechanical promise, current research falls short of translating these benefits into clinically meaningful outcomes. Future studies can consider targeting patients with relevant comorbidities, extend follow-up duration, and incorporate compliance and usability metrics to promote further integration of 3D-AFOs into routine clinical practice.

entry.title: The gait stability characteristics of individuals with chronic ankle instability.
entry.content:
Chen H, Kang Q, Yao M, Li D, et al. · Acta Orthop Traumatol Turc · 2026

The objective of this study was to investigate gait stability characteristics in patients with chronic ankle instability (CAI) by analyzing six degrees of freedom (6DOF) kinematic alterations in comparison with healthy controls. A cross-sectional study was conducted to evaluate 6DOF ankle kinematics in individuals with CAI and healthy controls using a dual fluoroscopic imaging system during treadmill walking. Three representative gait cycles were selected for each participant, normalized to 0-100% of the gait cycle, and averaged for analysis. Time-series kinematic differences were assessed using Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM1D) with one-way ANOVA and post-hoc tests, while discrete variables were compared between groups with Bonferroniadjusted significance. Compared with the control group, the contralateral limbs demonstrated greater distal displacement during 44-55% of the gait cycle (2.7-3.8 mm, p<0.001), whereas the CAI limbs exhibited reduced plantarflexion during 68-75% of the gait cycle (5.1-7.3, p<0.001). Additionally, the range of motion (ROM) for abduction-adduction (2.5Åã, p<0.05) and internal-external rotation (2.4, p<0.05) on the CAI sides was smaller compared with the contralateral sides. Both the CAI and contralateral limbs showed a decrease in medial-lateral displacement in the coronal plane relative to the control group (3.1mm, p<.05). This study demostrated that individuals with CAI exhibit distinct gait strategies compared to healthy controls, characterized by a reduction in plantarflexion in the CAI sides, an increase in distal displacement in the contralateral sides, and an overall decrease in the ROM on the CAI sides.   Cite this article as: Chen H, Kang Q, Yao M, et al. entry.title: Correlation analysis between ankle proprioception and biomechanical characteristics in patients with chronic ankle instability.
entry.content:
Guo P, Wang J · Acta Bioeng Biomech · 2026

To compare ankle proprioception and biomechanical features between individuals with chronic ankle instability (CAI) and healthy controls, and to investigate the interplay between proprioceptive deficits and biomechanical alterations in CAI. Thirty-six male participants (18 CAI, 18 healthy controls) were recruited. Proprioception was evaluated using a joint position reproduction test, quantifying absolute errors. For biomechanical assessment, participants performed six single-leg hopping tests. An infrared motion-capture system (Vicon T40, 200 Hz) and a force platform (Kistler, 1,000 Hz) simultaneously captured ankle kinematics/kinetics. Ankle muscle activation was recorded via surface electromyography (Noraxon, 2,000 Hz). Participants with CAI demonstrated significantly greater joint position sense errors in plantarflexion (P = 0.002), dorsiflexion (P = 0.001), inversion (P = 0.011), and eversion (P = 0.022) compared with controls. Compared with healthy controls, individuals with CAI exhibited greater peak ankle inversion angles (P = 0.039), reduced peak ankle dorsiflexion angles (P = 0.029), and lower activation of the tibialis anterior (P = 0.019) and peroneus longus (P = 0.033) during single-leg landing. Correlation analyses indicated significant associations between inversion position sense errors and both peak ankle dorsiflexion angle (r = -0.584, P = 0.011) and peak ankle inversion angle (r = -0.622, P = 0.006) in the CAI group. Individuals with CAI exhibit impaired ankle proprioception and altered biomechanical characteristics compared with healthy controls. Decreased proprioception in the ankle was correlated with biomechanical defects. These findings suggest that proprioceptive impairments may contribute to persistent biomechanical abnormalities in CAI. Comprehensive interventions targeting proprioceptive enhancement may improve ankle biomechanics in this population.

entry.title: Design and biomechanical investigation of a patient-specific total talar prosthesis for total talar replacement: A finite element analysis.
entry.content:
Tabrej MQ, Kumar A, Biswas JK · Int J Artif Organs · 2026

Total talar replacement (TTR) is an emerging treatment for end-stage talar diseases, although concerns persist regarding ankle stability due to essential ligament transection. Further investigation is necessary regarding the biomechanical impact of patient-specific total talar prosthesis (TTP) on ankle stability and bone-implant mechanics. The purpose of this study is designing a patient-specific TTP and assess its biomechanical performance on ankle stability and stress distribution under various loading conditions using finite element analysis. A CT scan is used to create a 3D finite element model of the foot and ankle complex. The TTP made of A dual-material (UHMWPE talar body and titanium alloy cage) was created and fixed with five screws. Four loading conditions were simulated: inversion, eversion, dorsiflexion, and plantarflexion, with forces of 10 N, 50 N, 100 N, and 150 N. Talar tilt angles and von Mises stresses were examined for intact and implanted models. In comparison to the intact ankle, TTR significantly decreased the talar tilt angles in inversion (12.5%-16%), eversion (6.6%-14%), and dorsiflexion (33%-47%). On the other hand, plantarflexion produced a larger tilt (34%-44%). While bone stresses stayed below 5 MPa, maximum implant stresses ranged from 20 to 80 MPa. The validation of the model against cadaveric studies was reliable. The patient-specific TTP with screw fixation improves ankle stability in most loading directions, potentially compensating for ligament insufficiency. However, greater plantarflexion instability necessitates post-operative measures. These findings provide biomechanical evidence that fixation-enhanced TTP designs can improve therapeutic outcomes.

entry.title: Position-Dependent Stability of an Unconstrained Total Talar Replacement and Its Suture Reinforcement: A Human Cadaveric Weight-Bearing Computed Tomography Study.
entry.content:
Raykov G, Penev P, Gehweiler D, Barcik J, et al. · Bioengineering (Basel) · 2026

Total talar replacement (TTR) is a joint-preserving alternative to arthrodesis in end-stage talar collapse. However, excising the talus detaches its anchoring ligaments and capsule, and unconstrained prosthesis constructs are prone to malalignment and dislocation. Moreover, it remains unclear whether the instability and its suture stabilisation vary across foot positions. Therefore, the aim of this study was to quantify the positional, load-dependent stability of an unconstrained TTR and the effect of its suture stabilisation. Five human cadaveric lower legs were imaged by weight-bearing computed tomography (CT) imaging in nine positions under 10 N and 700 N load in the intact condition and then with an unconstrained custom 3D-printed specimen-specific TTR, followed by supplementary transosseous suture stabilisation of the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) and deep tibiotalar deltoid in the third condition. In the intact ankle condition, load-induced displacements were minimal and unaffected by foot position, averaging no more than 0.52 mm and 0.62°. The unconstrained TTR exhibited position-dependent load-induced displacements, with talar shift increasing significantly by 2.29 mm in inversion and calcaneofibular distance decreasing significantly by 1.54 mm in eversion compared with the intact ankle condition (p ≤ 0.033). Suture stabilisation significantly decreased talar shift by 1.45 mm in inversion and significantly increased calcaneofibular distance by 1.37 mm in eversion, restoring these load-induced displacements toward the intact ankle condition (p = 0.002). In this human cadaveric weight-bearing CT imaging study, an unconstrained TTR benefited from suture reconstruction of the ATFL and deep tibiotalar deltoid attachments, highlighting the value of evaluating construct stability under load across the range of foot positions rather than in neutral stance alone.
